title: 1 Kings 16:15–28
context: Zimri reigns seven days before the army proclaims its commander Omri king; Zimri dies in the burning palace at Tirzah. After a period of civil division with Tibni, Omri takes sole rule, buys the hill of Samaria, and builds his capital there. Kings gives Omri a brief, negative notice. The dating in 16:23 appears to count from a different starting point than 16:15, and interpreters explain it in more than one way.

verses.text: In the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, Zimri reigned seven days in Tirzah. Now the people were encamped against Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines.
verses.arminianNotes: Zimri reigns seven days in Tirzah while the army besieges Gibbethon. Arminian readers note how fleeting power is when seized by violence. The army, not the capital, will decide who rules next.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the seven-day reign as a picture of the emptiness of usurpation. Zimri’s name later becomes a byword for a traitor (2 Kings 9:31).

verses.text: The people who were encamped heard that Zimri had conspired, and had also killed the king. Therefore all Israel made Omri, the captain of the army, king over Israel that day in the camp.
verses.arminianNotes: The army hears of the coup and makes Omri king that day. Arminian readers note that the people choose their own leader, a decision with long consequences.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe the speed with which events turn. God governs the rise and fall of kings even through the choices of soldiers in a camp.

verses.text: Omri went up from Gibbethon, and all Israel with him, and they besieged Tirzah.
verses.arminianNotes: Omri leads Israel from Gibbethon to besiege Tirzah. Arminian readers note the swift response of the army to the coup. Tirzah, the scene of Elah’s murder, now becomes the target of Omri’s siege, and the capital is quickly taken.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the siege of Gibbethon abandoned as Israel turns on itself. Civil strife distracts the nation from its external enemy. The Philistine town is left behind once again.

verses.text: When Zimri saw that the city was taken, he went into the fortified part of the king’s house and burned the king’s house over him with fire, and died,
verses.arminianNotes: Zimri, seeing the city taken, burns the palace over himself and dies. Arminian readers read his death soberly as despair at the end of a violent grasp for power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the narrator records the death without embellishment and attributes it to his sins. The usurper perishes in the house he seized.

verses.text: for his sins which he sinned in doing that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, in walking in the way of Jeroboam, and in his sin which he did to make Israel to sin.
verses.arminianNotes: Zimri’s death is attributed to his sins, walking in Jeroboam’s way. Arminian readers note that even in seven days a king could choose a direction for which he is accountable.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the refrain is applied even to a seven-day reign, showing how deeply Jeroboam’s pattern had shaped the northern kingdom. Even a usurper of a week is measured by the covenant.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Zimri, and his treason that he committed, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
verses.arminianNotes: Zimri’s acts and treason are recorded in the chronicles. Arminian readers note that he is remembered chiefly for betrayal. His conspiracy succeeded for only a week, and the record preserves that fact.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the word treason as the narrator’s verdict on Zimri’s brief reign. The record of his treason stands alongside the brief notice of his reign, a quiet reminder that betrayal does not become legitimate simply by succeeding.

verses.text: Then the people of Israel were divided into two parts: half of the people followed Tibni the son of Ginath, to make him king, and half followed Omri.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel divides between Tibni and Omri. Arminian readers see a nation torn by competing loyalties, each side choosing its leader. The division recalls, on a smaller scale, the split of the kingdom itself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the deepening instability of a kingdom without a covenant foundation. Division within division marks the north. Tibni is otherwise unknown, and the text gives no evaluation of him.

verses.text: But the people who followed Omri prevailed against the people who followed Tibni the son of Ginath; so Tibni died, and Omri reigned.
verses.arminianNotes: Omri’s supporters prevail, Tibni dies, and Omri reigns. Arminian readers note that the text does not say how Tibni died, and they avoid speculating. The narrator moves quickly to Omri’s reign.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that the civil war ends with Omri’s victory. God’s providence brings a measure of stability, though not faithfulness. Omri’s dynasty will last longer than any northern house before it.

verses.text: In the thirty-first year of Asa king of Judah, Omri began to reign over Israel for twelve years. He reigned six years in Tirzah.
verses.arminianNotes: Omri begins to reign in Asa’s thirty-first year for twelve years, six in Tirzah. Arminian readers note the brief notice of a significant reign. Moving from Tirzah later signals a new beginning for the dynasty.
verses.reformedNotes: Since Omri was proclaimed in Asa’s twenty-seventh year (16:15-16), many interpreters suggest the thirty-first year marks his sole rule after Tibni, with the twelve years counted from his acclamation. Reformed readers present this as a reasonable reconstruction rather than a certainty.

verses.text: He bought the hill Samaria of Shemer for two talents of silver; and he built on the hill, and called the name of the city which he built, Samaria, after the name of Shemer, the owner of the hill.
verses.arminianNotes: Omri buys the hill of Samaria for two talents of silver and builds his capital there. Arminian readers note the lasting effect of his decision, since Samaria remained Israel’s capital.
verses.reformedNotes: The WEB footnote gives a talent as about thirty kilograms. Reformed readers note that Samaria later becomes a symbol of Israel’s apostasy in the prophets, though here it is simply a royal city.

verses.text: Omri did that which was evil in the LORD’s sight, and dealt wickedly above all who were before him.
verses.arminianNotes: Omri did evil, worse than all before him. Arminian readers note that political success did not prevent spiritual decline. Worse than all before him is a strong verdict, given Jeroboam’s legacy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Kings measures kings by faithfulness, not achievement. Extrabiblical inscriptions are often cited as referring to Omri, but Kings is concerned only with his evil.

verses.text: For he walked in all the way of Jeroboam the son of Nebat, and in his sins with which he made Israel to sin, to provoke the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger with their vanities.
verses.arminianNotes: Omri walked in Jeroboam’s way, provoking the LORD with vanities. Arminian readers stress the continued choice of idolatry. His policies set the course that Ahab will intensify.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the pattern of sin solidifying across dynasties, preparing for Ahab’s still greater evil. The worthlessness of idols becomes a recurring theme in the prophets who follow.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Omri which he did, and his might that he showed, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
verses.arminianNotes: Omri’s deeds and might are referred to the royal annals. Arminian readers take the brief notice as a reminder that God weighs leaders by the faithfulness each is free to pursue, not by the power they gather. The narrator does not deny his might, but declines to dwell on it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the narrator’s restraint, focusing on the theological evaluation rather than political accomplishment. Achievement is acknowledged and then set aside in favor of the covenant verdict.

verses.text: So Omri slept with his fathers, and was buried in Samaria; and Ahab his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes: Omri dies and is buried in Samaria, and Ahab succeeds him. Arminian readers note that a new reign brings a new opportunity, though Ahab will choose worse.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the transition to Ahab as the beginning of a dark chapter, which God will meet by raising up Elijah. Samaria, the city Omri founded, becomes the seat of Ahab’s Baal worship (16:32).
